chapter_theme: The first half of the Vaazhthu Kaathai: a prose summary recalls Senguttuvan's northern campaign for the Himalaya stone and its consecration, then Kannaki's friends from Puhar arrive at her shrine and lament before the image, telling of the deaths of the mothers, the renunciations of both fathers, of Madhavi and Manimekalai, and of Maadhari's death for a broken charge; Kannaki appears in the sky, declares the Pandya faultless and herself his daughter, and the women of Vanchi sing her and bless both the Pandya and the Chera lines.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi, son of Cheralathan by a Chola princess, who brought the Himalaya stone for the pathini and consecrated it
Senguttuvan's father, the Chera who ruled the world from Kumari to the northern Himalaya
the northern Aryan kings whose taunt provoked the expedition and who were made to carry the stone on their heads
the great ascetics living in the north who brought word of the Aryan kings' taunt
Kovalan's wife, the pathini, now worshipped as a goddess at Vanchi and appearing in the sky
Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed and died of his own verdict (named here காவலன், தென்னவன், கோவேந்தன்)
the royal goldsmith of Madurai, called here the petty man
Kovalan's father, who renounced on hearing of the deaths
Kannaki's father, who also renounced
Kovalan's mother, Maasaathuvan's wife, who died of grief
Kannaki's mother, who died of grief
the dancer of Puhar, Kovalan's companion, who renounced before the Buddhist monks
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, who renounced with her
Kannaki's friend, the Brahmin woman who lived with the god Saathan
Kannaki's foster mother, who calls herself her தாயர்
Kannaki's personal maid-companion, daughter of the foster mother
the old herdswoman of Madurai to whom Kannaki was given in charge, dead of grief at failing that charge
Maadhari's unmarried daughter, who comes with the Puhar women to Vanchi
the Jain nun who placed Kannaki in Maadhari's charge, named here only by an epithet if that is the reading
the women of Vanchi who call one another to sing Kannaki
the company of women whose venba sets the two kings' claims to Kannaki side by side
Indra, king of the gods, whose palace receives the Pandya as guest

silappathikaram:29:1-20.reading: The prose opening tells how Senguttuvan, son of the world-ruling Cheralathan by the Chola's daughter, after the Kongu war and the Ganga campaign, heard from the northern ascetics that the Aryan kings had laughed that no crowned kings like themselves were left in the Tamil south, as on the day bow, tiger and fish were cut on the Himalaya's brow; stung, he routed them, made them carry the Himalaya stone on their crowned heads, bathed the lady in the Ganga, came back to Vanchi with his rage spent, and consecrated the image, worshipped by many kings' crowns, of the pathini as a goddess.
silappathikaram:29:1-20.nuance: The cause given is not devotion but a slight to Tamil kingship: the taunt touches the Chera's pride, and the stone for the goddess is quarried by humbling the kings who made it, so worship and conquest are one act. The ascetics are the ones who carry the word that starts a war. The stone is first called a stone that is to be a god (கற்கடவுள், line 13) and only after the Ganga bathing and consecration a படிமம் and a goddess; the poem marks the stages by which a stone becomes a deity. The three emblems carved on the Himalaya belong to the three Tamil crowns, not the Chera alone.
silappathikaram:29:1-20.unit_note: Moved the boundary from after line 16 to after line 20. Line 16 ends in the middle of the word கங்கைப்பேர் / யாற்று, which runs into line 17; the stone's journey and consecration close at கடவுண் மங்கலஞ்செய்த பின்னாள் on line 20, the next clause, Kannaki's shrine and the kings' tribute, begins with that line's last word கண்ணகி, which stays in this unit because no line end in the prose (lines 1 to 36) falls on a phrase break.
silappathikaram:29:1-20.event: Senguttuvan, told by northern ascetics of the Aryan kings' taunt, defeats them, makes them carry the Himalaya stone, bathes it in the Ganga and consecrates it at Vanchi as the pathini's image.

silappathikaram:29:21-36.reading: On a later day, as Senguttuvan was receiving the tribute of earthly kings at Kannaki's shrine, the women of Puhar came: the prose recalls how Kannaki, her moon face streaming with tears and her dark hair loose with dust, reviled dharma when Kovalan's deed rose up and the petty goldsmith had him killed, went to the king, and how the king lost his life at her tears; how Maasaathuvan, told by a Brahmin, renounced and his wife died; and how the foster mother, the maid and Devanthi went to Madurai to see Kannaki, met Maadhari's daughter Aiyai, and with her followed the Vaigai up the great hill to the queen's shrine, where they tell the king what happened.
silappathikaram:29:21-36.nuance: In one breath the prose names three causes of Kovalan's death: his own former deed rising up (வினையுருத்து), the goldsmith who brought it about (குறுமகனால்), and the king who caused the killing. Kannaki's response is to blame dharma itself (அறம்பழித்து), a protest the poem records without answering here. Maadhari is not named; she is the herding woman who died having lost the charge entrusted to her (அடைக்கலமிழந்து உயிரிழந்த, line 32). The shrine on the hill is reached by following the Vaigai, which ties the Vanchi cult back to Madurai.
silappathikaram:29:21-36.unit_note: Moved the boundary from after line 16 to after line 20 (see the unit 1-20); this unit begins with the clause about Kannaki's shrine and the kings' tribute (its first word கண்ணகி stands at the end of line 20), and ends at line 36, where the long prose sentence closes with திறமுரைப்பர் மன்.
silappathikaram:29:21-36.event: As Senguttuvan takes tribute at Kannaki's shrine, Kannaki's foster mother, maid and Devanthi, who went to Madurai and came on with Aiyai, arrive and tell him what befell.

claims.claim: a man's former deed rose up against him and brought his killing through a petty man

silappathikaram:29:37-41.reading: Devanthi tells the king to see in her the friend of the bangled one who was born on the divine northern Himalaya, guarded by the three crowned kings, and came after bathing in the swift Ganga: the friend of the doll of the Chola country.
silappathikaram:29:37-41.nuance: The words describe the stone as much as the woman: born in the Himalaya and bathed in the Ganga is the history of the image told in lines 1 to 20, and Devanthi speaks of it as Kannaki herself, so the image and the woman are one in her grief. The refrain names Kannaki by her home country, the Chola land.
silappathikaram:29:37-41.event: Devanthi, before the image, declares herself the friend of Kannaki.

silappathikaram:29:42-46.reading: The foster mother says she is the mother of the wide-eyed girl who, taking her loving husband's hand away from soft-mannered Madhavi without reproach, came through the cruel forest of wells no pot can reach: the mother of the doll of cool Puhar.
silappathikaram:29:42-46.nuance: கடம்படாள் is hard: it may mean that Kannaki did not hold Madhavi to account, or that she owed no duty to her; either way the line sets her taking back her husband apart from any quarrel with the dancer. தாயர் is the foster mother's own title, not birth.
silappathikaram:29:42-46.event: The foster mother declares herself Kannaki's mother.

silappathikaram:29:47-52.reading: Under the rubric 'the maid's word', the maid says that the gold-bangled lady who took chastity as her duty and followed her lover left without a word to the mother who bore her, to the foster mother who guarded her, or to the maid herself: she is that lady's friend, the friend of the doll of flowering Puhar.
silappathikaram:29:47-52.nuance: The grievance is that Kannaki left in secret; the same deed that the poem praises as chastity (கற்புக் கடம்பூண்டு) cost those at home a farewell. The phrase கற்புக் கடம்பூண்ட is the one Kavunthi used of Kannaki when she gave her into Maadhari's care (15:131-148, line 143).
silappathikaram:29:47-52.event: Kannaki's maid declares herself her friend and complains she left without a word.

silappathikaram:29:53-57.reading: Devanthi laments that she, who had done no penance, heard the ill dream and did not grasp what it would bring, and asks her friend whether she has heard that on the day of the outcry of her breast her mother died, and her mother-in-law too.
silappathikaram:29:53-57.nuance: Devanthi blames her own lack of penance (செய்தவம் இல்லாதேன்) for failing to read the dream; in the dream kaathai she had read it as the fruit of a vow broken in a former birth and prescribed a bath in the tanks, and now she owns that she did not see what it portended. முலைப்பூசல் names the burning of Madurai by the breast. The friend she addresses is Kannaki, now the image.
silappathikaram:29:53-57.event: Devanthi tells Kannaki that her mother and her mother-in-law died on hearing of the burning.

claims.claim: one who lacks the merit of penance cannot grasp what a dream foretells

silappathikaram:29:58-63.reading: Under the rubric 'the foster mother's lament', she asks whether Kannaki has heard that Maasaathuvan, grieving that the king gave up his life when the petty man brought about Kovalan's death, held that death itself was now his life, made many gifts and renounced, and that Maanaaygan renounced too.
silappathikaram:29:58-63.nuance: The renunciation is grief's, not doctrine's: the father turns away because life after the news is no life (சாவதுதான் வாழ்வு), and the gifts come as part of leaving the world. The cause of Kovalan's death is put on the petty man, and the king's death is what the father heard of.
silappathikaram:29:58-63.event: The foster mother tells Kannaki that both fathers, Maasaathuvan and Maanaaygan, gave gifts and renounced.

silappathikaram:29:64-68.reading: The maid asks whether Kannaki has heard that Madhavi, grieving at her lover's death and at Kannaki's fate and hearing the blame of strangers, made gifts of merit before the great ascetics under the Bodhi tree and renounced, and that Manimekalai renounced too.
silappathikaram:29:64-68.nuance: Madhavi's renunciation is placed under the Bodhi tree before the monks, a Buddhist setting, and is moved partly by what strangers say of her (ஏதிலார் ஏச்சுரை); the story the Manimekalai tells begins here. The text states the act, not a doctrine.
silappathikaram:29:64-68.event: The maid tells Kannaki that Madhavi and Manimekalai renounced before the monks under the Bodhi tree.

silappathikaram:29:69-73.reading: Devanthi, showing Aiyai, asks Kannaki whether she sees the unmarried girl with fine teeth, daughter of the mother who gave up her life saying she had fallen into madness because she could not guard the charge given her by the one of clear vision: the young daughter of her mother-in-law.
silappathikaram:29:69-73.nuance: ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி, 'of vision freed from doubt', seems to name Kavunthi, the Jain nun who gave Kannaki into Maadhari's care, though it could qualify the charge itself. Maadhari dies of the failure to keep a trust, not of any wrong she did. Calling Maadhari மாமி, mother-in-law, makes Aiyai a kinswoman by the bond of the charge; the kinship term is affectionate and its exact sense is not sure.
silappathikaram:29:69-73.event: Devanthi shows Aiyai to Kannaki and tells of Maadhari's death.

silappathikaram:29:74-77.reading: Senguttuvan cries out three times what this can be: a lightning creeper with a golden anklet, a girdle, bangled arms, fine diamond earrings and ornaments of Jambu gold appears high in the sky.
silappathikaram:29:74-77.nuance: The king sees first only a flash of jewels and lightning, not a person; the anklet is the first ornament named, the thing the story turned on.
silappathikaram:29:74-77.event: Kannaki appears in the sky as a lightning-like figure in jewels, and Senguttuvan cries out in wonder.

silappathikaram:29:78-83.reading: Under the rubric 'Kannaki shows Senguttuvan her goddess's form', Kannaki says that the Pandya is without fault and has become a welcome guest in the palace of the king of the gods; she is his daughter; she will not leave the playground on the hill of the one of the victorious spear; and she calls her friends to come with her.
silappathikaram:29:78-83.nuance: This is the sharpest turn in the epic's judgment of the king: the woman who called him a king who strayed from right rule and burned his city now declares him faultless and claims him as father. His self-sentence and death have cleared him. The hill of the spear-bearer is Murugan's, near where the kuravar saw her taken up.
silappathikaram:29:78-83.event: Kannaki, appearing as a goddess, tells Senguttuvan the Pandya is faultless and in Indra's palace, and calls her friends.

claims.claim: a king who gave up his life for his own wrong verdict is free of fault and received among the gods

silappathikaram:29:84-92.reading: The women of Vanchi call one another, women with waists like the vanchi creeper and companions of the fierce-speared king, to come and sing her who with her breast ruined the city of Koodal and with her red anklet overcame the king, the Pandya's daughter, the bangled doll who came to this land when our king's just tongue declared that Pandyas do not live once the sceptre bends.
silappathikaram:29:84-92.nuance: The songs praise Kannaki for destroying a city and defeating a king, and in the same stanza they call her that king's daughter, taking up her own claim. The saying about the Pandyas is put in the mouth of the Chera king (எங்கோ முறைநா), so a rival line honours the Pandyas for dying of their own injustice.

claims.claim: Pandya kings do not live on once their sceptre bends

silappathikaram:29:93-96.reading: A venba says that while we called her the daughter of our king the Chera, she called herself the creeper born of the king of the Vaigai's people; so let us praise the Chera, and the divine woman will praise the lord of the Vaigai.
silappathikaram:29:93-96.nuance: Two kings claim one goddess, and the dispute is settled by dividing the praise: the people of Vanchi keep their own king, and the goddess keeps the Pandya, the king who wronged her.

silappathikaram:29:97-100.reading: Long live the great king who gave his life when the tears of her who suffered by an old deed killed him, long live the ancient line of the lord of Madurai, circled by the Vaigai's flowing water.
silappathikaram:29:97-100.nuance: Both causes stand in one line: her suffering came by an old deed (தொல்லை வினையால்), and the king died of her tears. The blessing falls on the king who caused the wrong, praised for paying with his life, and on his whole line. Who sings these stanzas is not named; they follow the women's songs.

claims.claim: her suffering came from a deed of old
a king who gives up his life for a wrong done under him is to be praised

silappathikaram:29:101-104.reading: Long live the king who set the young doll born of the mountain king on the long crowns of the kings of the earth, long live the ancient line of the lord of Vanchi, circled by the cool Porunai.
silappathikaram:29:101-104.nuance: மலையரையன் பெற்ற மடப்பாவை fits both the Himalaya stone and the mountain king's daughter, the goddess Uma, so the image is praised in a goddess's terms; the doll set on kings' crowns recalls the defeated kings made to carry the stone. The stanza answers the Pandya's blessing line for line.

links.note: The decade preface on Senguttuvan, son of Nedunjeralathan by the Chola Manakkilli, says in one phrase that he went north wanting a stone for the goddess pathini and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's prose gives the same parentage and campaign, and adds the Aryan kings' taunt and the stone carried on their heads.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the Sangam colophon tradition already knew a Chera king's northern stone for a pathini, and the epic turns that bare record into a cause and a ritual: the stone becomes a goddess only after it is won by humbling the kings who mocked Tamil kingship.

gains.a: the epic's prose gains an outside witness for the king's parentage and his stone-seeking campaign, so the cult is set in remembered Chera history
gains.b: the preface's terse phrase கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains the story of whose stone it was and why the king went for it

links.note: The second decade's preface credits Imayavaramban Nedunjeralathan with carving the bow on the Himalaya; the epic's Aryan kings recall the day bow, tiger and fish were all carved there, and say no such kings are left.
links.teaches: The epic widens one Chera's boast into the shared emblem of the three Tamil crowns and makes the memory a reproach, so the son's campaign is shown as the redeeming of a glory the north said had lapsed.

gains.a: the taunt's 'day the bow was carved' gains a named Chera, Senguttuvan's own father, as its author
gains.b: the preface's single deed gains a later afterlife as a standard that northern kings could throw back at his heirs

links.note: Neeli's curse in the former birth is the deed the prose says rose up against Kovalan (வினையுருத்து); the prose also names the goldsmith and the king.
links.teaches: The retelling at Vanchi keeps the goddess's karmic explanation but sets it beside the petty man and the king as agents, and beside Kannaki's reviling of dharma, so the karmic cause is told without excusing the human ones.

links.note: In the dream kaathai Devanthi read Kannaki's dream as the fruit of a vow broken in a former birth and prescribed a bath in the tanks; here she says she heard the dream and did not grasp what it would bring.
links.teaches: The friend who once explained the dream by past karma and a ritual remedy now confesses she misread it, so her earlier karmic diagnosis is shown to have been the wrong kind of answer to a warning of the future.

links.note: The quatrain says the best renounce without delay after slowly considering that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last; Maasaathuvan gives his wealth away and renounces only when the news of his son's death makes life seem death.
links.teaches: The pair separates renunciation reached by reflection from renunciation forced by bereavement: the epic's fathers come to the quatrain's act by the road the quatrain hopes to spare, after the loss has already happened.

gains.a: the father's turning gains a measure: it is the right act done late, under grief rather than insight
gains.b: the quatrain's counsel gains a case showing what the delay it warns against costs, a house emptied before its master leaves it

links.note: Kavunthi told Maadhari that a charge held for the ascetics, however small, yields very great joy; Maadhari, who could not guard that charge, gave up her life.
links.teaches: The promise of joy from keeping a trust is reversed into death from failing it, and the failure was not hers: the pair shows the epic laying on a guardian the full weight of a duty that the king's act made impossible to keep.

links.note: At the palace gate Kannaki called the Pandya a king of ruined sense who strayed from right rule (இறைமுறை பிழைத்தோன்); in the sky she calls him faultless (தீதிலன்) and herself his daughter.
links.teaches: The same speaker gives opposite verdicts on the same king, and the epic means both: the turn shows that in its eyes the king's death of his own sentence has cancelled the fault she rightly charged him with.

links.note: The king's own sentence, யானோ அரசன் யானே கள்வன், and his death are what Kannaki now rewards by declaring him Indra's guest.
links.teaches: Read together, the scenes show the self-condemnation as the act that wins the king heaven: the confession that he was the thief is what makes him faultless in the goddess's word.

links.note: The couplet says a ruler endures by just rule and without it his lustre does not endure; the Vanchi women sing that Pandyas do not live once the sceptre bends, and praise the Pandya for that.
links.teaches: The epic grants the couplet's link between a bent sceptre and the king's end but reverses its outcome for fame: the Pandya's dying of his own injustice is exactly what makes his line's glory endure and be sung by a rival kingdom.

gains.a: the women's saying gains a general rule behind it, so the Pandya's death reads as the law of kingship and not a private collapse
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where losing life for a bent sceptre restores the lustre it says is lost, a limit on its simple equation

links.note: The patikam's morals are that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship and that an old deed comes to make its doer eat its fruit; the blessing names the old deed as the cause of her suffering and hails the king dharma killed.
links.teaches: The closing blessing keeps both of the patikam's causes but changes the moral's tone: the king to whom dharma became death is not left as a warning but praised with his whole line, because he died of it.

links.note: Devanthi's friend born on the Himalaya and bathed in the Ganga and the blessing's doll born of the mountain king are the same Himalaya stone, spoken of as Kannaki.
links.teaches: The Himalaya origin is given to Kannaki twice, once in a friend's grief and once in a royal blessing, and the second, with its echo of the mountain king's daughter, shows the woman of Puhar being absorbed into the figure of the great goddess.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the epic's own word (patikam line 56, here கடவுள் பத்தினி only by implication); declared earlier in silappathikaram ch001

new_concepts.gloss: a blessing or praise-song wishing long life to a king, a god or a line
new_concepts.label_source: the kaathai's title and the block rubric வாழ்த்து; the stanzas' refrain வாழியரோ

new_concepts.gloss: tribute paid by subject or defeated kings

source_issues: Block labels misplace three rubrics: the block காவற்பெண்டு சொல் (42-52) contains the rubric அடித் தோழி சொல் at line 47, so lines 48-52 are the maid's speech; the block தேவந்தி யரற்று (53-63) contains the rubric காவற்பெண் டரற்று at line 58, so 59-63 are the foster mother's; the block செங்குட்டுவன் கூற்று (74-83) contains the rubric at lines 78-79 (செங்குட்டுவற்குக் கண்ணகியார் கடவு ணல்லணி காட்டியது), so 80-83 are Kannaki's words. The rubric lines are counted as verse lines.

Lines 1-36 are prose (உரைப் பாட்டு மடை) broken into lines of the edition's own making, with words split across line ends (16-17 கங்கைப்பேர் / யாற்று, 18-19 நீண் / முடி, 19-20 பூச / லாட்டி, 25-26 மன் / னரசர், 27-28 துறப் / பவும்).
The kaathai header reports the printed last line as None.
